hero.title: Organic food labels: what the seal promises and what the evidence shows.
hero.lede: Wellness doctors say organic is more nutritious, prevents cancer and keeps poison off your plate. Skeptics call the label a marketing scam. This page pulls the testable claims out of videos and articles on both sides and checks each one against the USDA organic rules, the big meta-analyses and cohort studies, and government residue data.

recap.bottomLine: the organic seal reliably means what the rules say: at least 95% organic ingredients, no genetic engineering, no antibiotics or added hormones, three years off prohibited inputs. It does not mean no pesticides; approved ones are allowed and residues up to 5% of the EPA limit are legal. Organic produce does carry fewer residues, and switching diets cuts the pesticide levels in your urine within days, but residues on conventional produce sit far below safety limits, and no study shows that eating organic makes people healthier. The largest cancer cohort found no reduction. Organic crops carry more polyphenols and less cadmium, and organic milk more omega-3, mostly because the cows graze; overall nutrition is a wash. Organic costs clearly more, yields about a fifth less per acre, and per unit of food emits about as much greenhouse gas. {hypeWrong} of {hypeTotal} sweeping claims ("no pesticides", "only organic avoids harmful residues", "pesticides cause mass deaths") are judged wrong.
